sections.sectionText: Topic: “POPULAR MUSIC AND POWER.” This course reveals the connections between popular music and political power; examines how music furthers the interests of both governments and protest movements; considers the use of music in political campaigns; and explores the intersections between music and politics of gender, left- and right-wing ideologies, post-colonialism, race, sexuality, and warfare. In this class, we will discuss examples of folk music, glam rock, gospel, hip hop, punk rock, reggae, rhythm & blues, salsa, and soul in their societal context.

sections.sectionText: This course will engage with improvisatory technique in Western Europe from ca. 1500 to ca. 1700, with particular emphasis on the period surrounding the turn of the 17th century. Students will examine primary sources including contemporary musical examples and commentary on style and technique, as well as modern scholarship. In addition to engaging practically with musical examples in the classroom, students will have the opportunity to compose their own pseudo-improvisation over popular 16th-century pieces.

sections.sectionText: This course is intended to develop the student’s understanding of the intertwined relationship of recorded media, live performances, and artistic agency in the American popular music industry from the beginning of the twentieth century to the present. Focusing on critical case studies, the student will have the opportunity to get to know how genre categories and technology shape listening habits, engage with the general history of the music industry, better understand how copyright law disenfranchises artists from marginalized communities, and acquire the skills to craft grant proposals and program notes.

sections.sectionText: Topic: "THE CULTURAL STUDY OF JAZZ." This seminar will introduce students to the academic study of jazz. Its aims are twofold. First, we will explore how scholars have endeavored to study the music in itself: writing and debating its history, challenging its stylistic or national borders, or exploring the social relations that are built on and off the bandstand and that animate jazz as a practice. Second, we will consider jazz as a significant part of American culture, as well as its many echoes around the world. This includes thinking about jazz’s connections to other art forms, its entanglements with racial and gender ideology, or its participation in American imperialism, among many other things. While we will focus on jazz, this seminar will introduce students to issues and methodologies that are applicable to the study of popular music broadly speaking. Students are not expected to have prior knowledge of jazz history, to be fluent readers of Western music notation, or to know how to play an instrument. Final projects include research and creative options.

sections.sectionText: Topic: "AMERICAN MUSIC HISTORIOGRAPHY AND PEDAGOGY." This course is designed to prepare students to research and teach topics in American music studies. The study of American music has expanded from emphasis on musicians and musical practices in the continental United States to a more inclusive framework addressing music making throughout the Americas and around the world. The course features a dual emphasis on historiography, the ways that the history of American music has been written, and pedagogy, the ways that history has been taught. To that end, students will compare approaches to writing American music history, explore articles and journals devoted to American music, and apply the knowledge gained from that to prepare an undergraduate course. The course preparation will include the creation of a syllabus, the selection of readings and listening for sample class meetings, and the leadership of one of those class meetings—many of the things search committees require of faculty job candidates.
